Instructions for submitting Observer reports 

Introduction 
This document provides the reporting template and instructions for Observers to report 

during the 2023 - 2025 Norwegian Chairship of the Arctic Council. 

The deadline for submission is 1 December 2024. 

 

Role of Observers 
The role and responsibilities of Observers, as well as criteria for admission to the Arctic 

Council, can be found in the “Arctic Council Rules of Procedure” (Annex 2) and the 

“Observer Manual for Subsidiary Bodies.” 

The primary role of Observers is to observe the work of the Arctic Council. Observers 
contribute to the Arctic Council primarily through engagement at the level of Working 
Groups, Task Forces, and/or Expert Groups. Observers are invited to the meetings and 
other activities of the Arctic Council unless the Senior Arctic Officials decide otherwise. 
Observers may also propose projects through an Arctic State or a Permanent Participant. 

Report submission 
Observer reports should include the relevant information described below and in the 
template. 

(a) A description of the Observer’s contributions to the work of the Arctic Council since 
the time of the Observer’s most recent submission, or in the previous two years, with 
special focus on contributions to the subsidiary bodies through project participation 
and support, as well as collaboration with Permanent Participants; 

(b) If applicable, a description of the Observer’s future plans to contribute to the work of 
the Arctic Council, with special focus on contributions to the subsidiary bodies 
through project participation and support, as well as collaboration with Permanent 
Participants; and, 

(c) If applicable, a description of the Observer’s contributions to other aspects of the 
Arctic Council and its goals not covered in the previous sections since the time of the 
Observer’s most recent submission, or in the previous two years. 

 

Observer reports should be submitted electronically to the Arctic Council Secretariat via 

email: acs@arctic-council.org not later than 1 December 2024. Please bear in mind while 

preparing your report that all Observer reports will be published online in the Observer 

section of the Arctic Council online Library (OAR) following the Chairship transition. 

If an Observer fails to submit a report, the Arctic Council will consider this to mean that the 
Observer is no longer interested in maintaining its status as an accredited Observer to 
the Arctic Council.

Observer Report 
Please describe in no more than two pages your State’s or Organization’s contributions to 
the work of the Arctic Council’s Working Groups, Task Forces, and/or Expert Groups since 
the time of your most recent report, or in the previous two years. Please highlight 
contributions to specific projects, such as through proposals, concept development, in- 
kind and financial support, and hosting of meetings. Please detail any collaboration with 
Permanent Participants, such as project proposal endorsement and support. 

The Arctic matters to the United Kingdom. Although not an Arctic State, the UK is geographically 
proximate to the region. The future of the Arctic is therefore critical for UK interests and the UK 
has a lot to offer the region. The UK fully respects the sovereign rights of the Arctic States and 
Indigenous People of the Arctic, and we are pleased to play our part in scientific collaboration, 
regional cooperation and governance to promote a peaceful, sustainable and prosperous future 
for the Arctic. The UK is committed to the Arctic Council through our role as a State Observer, 
recognising its important role as the pre-eminent intergovernmental forum for Arctic co-operation. 
 
The UK has a longstanding connection to the Arctic, having previously been accredited as an 
Observer at the first Arctic Environmental Protection Strategy meeting in 1991, and for the Arctic 
Council since 1996. Officials from the Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office have 
represented the UK at each of the Senior Arctic Officials and Ministerial meetings of the Council 
since 1996 and continue to provide constructive engagement with the Council’s work including 
participating in the regular outreach meetings with Observers hosted by the Chairship. 
 
Despite the pause in much Arctic Council activity over the past two years the UK has actively 
engaged in Arctic research and contributed to the objectives of the Arctic Council as well as to the 
wider range of international treaties and organisations that pertain to the Arctic. In his recent 
speech to the Arctic Circle Assembly, the Minister for the Polar Regions, Stephen Doughty MP, 
reiterated the commitment of the new UK Government to the Arctic Council, noting the important 
role the Council has to play in articulating a strong voice for, and delivering effective governance 
in, the region. The UK remains guided by its Arctic Policy Framework, Looking North, which was 
updated and republished in 2023, and provides an overview of our objectives and contributions. 
The devolved Scottish Government has also continued to implement its 2019 Arctic Connections 
policy framework, which closely aligns with Arctic Council goals, particularly on shared challenges 
around climate and sustainable social development. The Arctic Connections framework is now 
entering its evaluation phase. 
 
With a view to supporting the work of the Arctic Council’s Working Groups as they resume 
business under the Norwegian Chairship, the UK has provided funding for the development of 
new projects and collaborations between UK and Arctic State researchers and the Arctic Council’s 
Working Groups. The Department for Science, Innovation and Technology and Foreign, 
Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO) have allocated combined funding of £710,000 to 
the Arctic Council Working Groups – UK Engagement Scheme 2024/25 which seeks to increase 
engagement between UK and Arctic State based researchers and the Arctic Council Working 
Groups. This scheme has been promoted in close collaboration with the Norwegian Chairship 
and Working Group representatives including through a side-event at Arctic Frontiers 2024. This 
funding has led to the approval of 11 research projects primarily supporting activities and 
engagement with AMAP, CAFF and PAME working groups, to help shape and support their future 
work programmes and contribute to the wider body of research vital to informing policy on the 
future of the region at this critical time. 
 
Alongside this scheme, UK representatives have continued to engage across a range of Arctic 
Council interests, contributing to the work of a large number of working and expert groups. This 
has included engagement in AMAP activities in areas such as litter, microplastics and climate

change, in PAME including in relation to shipping and plastic pollution, in CAFF on seabirds, and 
contributing to the Arctic Council’s Expert Group on Black Carbon and Methane. UK-based 
researchers have also contributed to events on the Norwegian Chairship’s Wildland Fire Initiative. 
 
The UK’s Natural Environment Research Council’s Arctic Office, Science and Innovation Network 
and FCDO’s Polar Regions Department have undertaken a range of initiatives to raise awareness 
of the Arctic Council Working Groups in the UK Arctic Science Community, reporting back on 
funded projects and contributing to wider dialogues. At Arctic Frontiers 2024 a 20-person UK 
science delegation helped strengthened collaborations, including through a UK hosted session 
with the Norwegian Chairship and AMAP to share experience of working with Working Groups. 
 
Over the past 18 months the UK has launched three other research partnership schemes directly 
with Arctic States or State Observers to the Arctic Council. These include the United Kingdom – 
Iceland Arctic Science Partnership Scheme, the United Kingdom and Greenland Arctic Bursary 
Scheme 2024/2025, and the United Kingdom and Japan Arctic Bursary Scheme 2024/2025. 
These will all address pressing research questions which will strengthen the scientific knowledge 
base of the Arctic community and be of direct relevance to the work of the Arctic Council Working 
Groups. Additionally, the Scottish Government supported 31 projects from 2021-2024 through the 
Arctic Connections Fund to enable Scottish organisations to collaborate with Arctic partners. 
 
The UK has hosted a number of events at Arctic fora involving Arctic Council and/or Working 
Group representatives. In addition to the session highlighted above, these events have included: 

• Arctic Circle Assembly, Iceland (October 2023): UK hosted sessions on UK-Greenland and 
UK-Iceland bursaries, and scoping meetings with Council and Working Group representatives. 

• Arctic Science Summit Week, Edinburgh, UK (March 2024): the second time in the UK, and 
first in Scotland. 900 participants from 35 countries made this the biggest UK Arctic gathering. 
The UK also hosted several side events. 

• Arctic Circle Berlin Forum, Germany (May 2024): plenary event on the scientific contributions 
of Observers to the Arctic Council with Observer representatives and Norwegian Chairship. 

• Arctic Circle Assembly (October 2024): UK/DE hosted session on the implications of a 
changing Arctic for science, policy and diplomacy involving Arctic State, Indigenous, and 
Observer State representation, and side event on UK-Iceland bursaries. 

 
Migratory species highlight the strong links between the UK and the Arctic. The UK’s Joint Nature 
Conservation Committee contributes to CAFF’s Circumpolar Seabird Expert Group (CBird) and to 
the Arctic Migratory Birds Initiative. This includes contributions to an Atlantic-wide assessment of 
the status, trends and drivers of Leach’s and European Storm-Petrel populations to understand 
demographic trends and environmental impacts on these species. The recent Seabirds Count 
census of all the UK's breeding seabird species is also supporting various CBird priority actions 
and providing geographic context to population trends of seabird species whose ranges span the 
UK and the Arctic. We are also supporting implementation of the Circumpolar Biodiversity 
Monitoring Programme and implementing African Eurasian Waterbird Agreement International 
Single Species Action Plans. UK contributions to OSPAR (the Convention for the Protection of 
the Marine Environment of the North-East Atlantic) will also benefit marine birds in the Arctic; the 
UK led the preparation of OSPAR Recommendation 2024/02 on reducing bycatch of marine birds 
in the maritime area, which was adopted by Parties in June 2024, as was OSPAR’s response to 
poor status of marine bird populations set out in its Regional Action Plan on Marine Birds. 
 
Finally, HM Coastguard (UK Maritime and Coastguard Agency) has contributed to the work of the 
Emergency Prevention, Preparedness and Response Working Group by attending the Plenary as 
well as the Search and Rescue and Marine Environmental Response Expert Groups, 
strengthening existing partnerships and developing new connections that will enable further 
sharing of knowledge and enhance cooperation in search and rescue and marine environmental 
response matters, essential preparedness as tourism and shipping visits to the Arctic increase.

If applicable, please describe in no more than one page your State’s or Organization’s 
future plans for contributing to the work of the Arctic Council’s Working Groups, Task 
Forces, and/or Expert Groups. Please highlight intentions to contribute to specific projects 
and to collaborate with Permanent Participants. 

 

The UK has invested over £135m in Arctic research over the last decade, including through UK 
centres of expertise. That investment in Arctic science and research is set to continue, with the 
new bursary schemes announced in 2024 and which are currently underway. The most recent of 
these is the Arctic Council Working Groups – UK Engagement Scheme 2024/2025, on which we 
will be reporting in a joint session with the Arctic Council Secretariat, UiT and AMAP at Arctic 
Frontiers 2025. During this session we also hope to explore the ways in which we can strengthen 
the interface between science and policy to support a sustained and increased contribution to the 
work of the Working Groups by researchers in the UK and beyond. 
 
We will also look to provide updates of progress on the other bursary schemes being run by the 
UK as their research progresses, at Arctic Frontiers and other fora and will be hosting an online 
information and networking session in December 2024 with the Arctic Council secretariat, 
representatives from the six working groups and UK researchers. 
 
These schemes build on bursaries run since 2017, including the 2021-2025 partnership with 
Canada and Inuit Nunangat, the Canada-Inuit Nunangat-United Kingdom (CINUK) Arctic 
Research Programme, which is a partnership between UKRI and Polar Knowledge Canada, 
National Research Council of Canada, Fonds de Recherche du Quebec, Parks Canada, and Inuit 
Tapiriit Kanatami. While this project is due to finish in 2025, it has set a new baseline for the way 
that modern science and indigenous knowledge can be brought together; we will be reviewing the 
outcomes of this programme in 2025 and our ambition is to use this as a framework for future 
collaboration with Indigenous People in the Arctic. 
 
With this promotion of Arctic research it is perhaps inevitable that this year saw the UK’s busiest 
research season at Ny-Ålesund, while the UK’s new Royal Research Ship, Sir David Attenborough, 
paid its first visit to the Arctic, to Greenland. The data gathered in this research is collaborative and 
will help us understand crucial changes and their impacts on the Arctic Ocean and beyond. Now, 
our Advanced Research and Invention Agency has launched an £81m call for proposals for further 
research programme around Greenland. This new programme seeks to test the proof of concept 
for the development an early warning system for ‘tipping points’, providing climate data of local and 
global importance. It will work closely with the local community in Greenland as well as international 
partners. 
 
This investment in science in support of the objectives of the Arctic Council has contributed to the 
UK recording the highest number of Arctic Council projects of any Observer State, while according 
to UArctic UK research continues to have the highest field-weighted citation impact in an analysis 
of the largest Arctic research nations between 2016-2021 (Rapprt). Finally, the UK is developing 
additional guidelines for UK researchers working in the Arctic in the shape of a Code of Conduct for 
the Arctic. This will accompany existing guidance and cover a range of issues including good 
practice in engaging with Indigenous People and local communities. 
 
We applaud the work of Norway during their Chairship to re-start technical collaboration under the 
Arctic Council first via written format and now virtual meetings. We look forward to working with the 
new Kingdom of Denmark Chairship of the Arctic Council from 2025, and to supporting the 
implementation of the Chairship’s objectives.

If applicable, please describe in no more than one page your State’s or Organization’s 
contributions to other aspects of the Arctic Council and its goals not covered by the 
previous sections since the time of your most recent report, or in the previous two years. 

The UK is engaged in a range of wider fora and issues where it is pursing activity relevant to the 
objectives of the Arctic Council including in relation to the International Maritime Organisation, 
OSPAR, and G7. For example, the UK has been supporting international coordination of research 
and innovation of relevance to the Arctic Ocean by lending support, via the G7 Future of the Seas 
and Ocean Initiative working group, to the Sustaining Arctic Observing Networks project’s 
proposal to develop an Arctic Ocean Regional Alliance, and actively participating in the All-Atlantic 
Ocean Research and Innovation Alliance, which has a pole-to-pole Atlantic Ocean footprint. 
 
The UK Met Office-led Advancing Arctic meteorological and oceanographic Capabilities (AAC) 
programme brings together international partners, which include Finland, Canada, USA, Norway, 
Sweden and Denmark, to develop an improved understanding of what is happening to the Arctic’s 
ice, ocean and atmosphere to support global climate resilience. The programme is funded under 
the International Science Partnerships Fund and has been allocated £4.98m to 2025. The AAC 
project aims to improve understanding of Arctic meteorology and oceanography, deliver a world-
class Arctic meteorological advice, and work closely with many partners and countries. 

 
The UK’s National Oceanography Centre (NOC) is currently strengthening and growing 
collaborations with Arctic States, and through their unique offerings lead and add value to major 
national and international Arctic initiatives. NOC operates two Royal Research Ships which were 
both undertaking Arctic science this year, including around Greenland where they engaged with 
the Greenlandic community and supported local search and rescue collaboration. NOC is also 
involved in a number of active research projects that contribute to the advancement of Arctic 
understanding. This includes partnering with the British Antarctic Survey-led “BIOPOLE” project 
that has been facilitated through partnerships with researchers in the United States, Canada, 
Norway, the Kingdom of Denmark and Germany. BIOPOLE is addressing the question of how 
climate change at both poles is affecting the availability of nutrients and the storage of carbon by 
the global ocean. 
 
The UK Maritime Coastguard Agency is currently undertaking work to implement the International 
Maritime Organization amendments to the Polar Code into UK regulations, which will come into 
force in January 2026. This brings into scope, fishing vessels >24m, cargo vessels 300-500GT 
and pleasure yachts >300GT who will have to comply with certain sections of the Polar Code. 
Additionally, HM Coastguard is an associate partner in the EU Interreg Northern Perimeter and 
Arctic Programme funded project on the development of Mass Rescue Operation Guidelines for 
the North Atlantic and Arctic. HM Coastguard also participated as partner in two EU Horizon 2020 
funded projects (AI-ARC - Artificial Intelligence based Virtual Control Room for the Arctic and 
ARCSAR - Arctic and North Atlantic Security and Emergency Preparedness Network) which 
concluded in February 2024. While the ARCSAR project provides a platform to prepare for coping 
with security and safety threats resulting from increased commercial activity in the Arctic region, 
the AI-ARC project developed a shared collaboration workspace based on innovative and efficient 
Artificial Intelligence services to enhance border and external security through cooperation in the 
Arctic and High North Sea region. 
 
The UK is seeking to join the Central Arctic Oceans Fisheries Agreement (CAOFA) at the earliest 
opportunity. We remain committed to working with our Arctic partners to ensure healthy marine 
ecosystems and future sustainable fishing in the region and are keen to contribute to relevant 
scientific research and monitoring. We have recently renewed our Observer status and will 
continue to observe CAOFA, where possible, until such a time we can join.
